newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian reform head sees improved living standards.
newsitem.headline: Russian reform head sees improved living standards.

text.p: Russians can look forward next year to the first improvement in living standards since the collapse of communism, thanks to a bold new reformist line taken by the government, the cabinet's economic chief said on Friday.
The millions of people whose lives have been blighted by the economic slump of the past six years have heard that line before, and will take some convincing the economy can grow in 1998.

But First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who is also finance minister, said that three months into what he called the most reform-minded Russian cabinet ever, he could already see results, and urged the government's opponents in the communist-dominated parliament not to get in their way.

"If nothing extraordinary happens...next year in Russia will be the first year of economic growth and the first year of an improvement in living standards," Chubais told a news conference. Officials had forecast two percent growth this year.
He also announced plans to begin long-term reforms of Russia's "fantastically inefficient" welfare system, including support for crumbling healthcare institutions.
And he forecast that the Russian stock market could boom thanks to efforts to clarify investment rules to attract funds.

"The growth of the Russian stock market is possible, not by percentage points, not by a number of times, but tens of times," Chubais said. "We are talking about hundreds of billions of dollars of potential growth...of the Russian equities market."

Chubais, 41, who won the enmity of communists when he spearheaded the mass privatisation drive of the early 1990s, was promoted three months ago after a spell as chief aide to President Boris Yeltsin following his re-election last July.

Yeltsin, recovering from months of illness, entrusted Chubais, under veteran Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, with a new wave of reforms designed to regain the support of ordinary Russians who have become disillusioned with daily hardships and the often corrupt wealth of a small elite.

"I think we've had a number of important results," he said, highlighting the drafting of a new tax code, which he said would cut the overall tax burden while introducing much-needed consistency and transparency to the present web of regulations.

The tax code is an integral part of the 1998 budget which the government wants to put through parliament this summer. It follows a flawed compromise finance act passed this year, which has already had to be corrected with massive spending cuts after tax income fell 47 percent below target.
Many officials are pessimistic it will be passed this year.

Bracing for a battle with the uncooperative State Duma lower house of parliament, Chubais urged deputies to at least make clear policy initiatives and avoid what frustrated ministers see as the simple delaying tactics it has used before.
"Parliaments have to make laws," Chubais said. "We need decisions from the Duma. What we can't accept is some kind of permanent delay...We demand that Duma express its position."

Resigned to personal unpopularity, Chubais launched a pre-emptive strike on the latest sleaze allegations against him. He said a letter would be published next week purporting to be from a foreign businessman and accusing him of taking bribes.
But, Chubais said, the businessman had already alerted the police to the forgery by his political enemies. "They're very productive. I don't think they'll stop now," he said.

Elaborating on results of the new reforms, Chubais noted that the giant gas monopoly Gazprom -- once headed by Chernomyrdin and the state's biggest debtor -- would pay off all it owed to the federal budget by the end of June.
Progress was also being made with other monopolies, notably the electricity distribution system and the railways.

Next in Chubais's sights was the social security system. He said the government could only afford to meet a fraction of its social commitments and much of the money spent was going to "stupid and senseless" payments to those who did not need it.

The crumbling health system would also be tackled later this year, although Chubais warned its problems could not be remedied in a couple of months. He denied the latest cuts affected real spending on health care, saying the savings were purely on paper.
